item.title: Societal Impacts Research on AI (SIRA)
item.description:
TL;DR: I'm launching Societal Impacts Research on AI (SIRA), a mentored research fellowship to bring more social science talent into AI safety. We're looking for our first cohort of 15-20 social scientists, from undergrads to postdocs, to work on societal impact problems within AI safety. The first cohort is projected to start in Summer 2027. Express interest as a fellow or mentor, or as a host organization or funder.

Introduction

The Industrial Revolution spawned the birth of modern social science to explain how industrialization was reshaping work, institutions, and social life. Coming forth as a response meant that the frameworks social science aimed to answer operated after the fact, leading to a near-universal game of catch-up in making sense of the moment. Today, Artificial Intelligence is proving to be a disruption of a similar (or even larger) scale, and if this technology continues to arrive faster than we can explain and understand its impact, humanity can miss the opportunity to better steer its development and deployment. I believe that humanity needs researchers - specifically social scientists - to study AI's effects on people and institutions while there is still time to shape the transition into a world of coexistence.[1]

Currently, social scientists who want to work on AI safety have no legible way in, except two weak options:

  1. Graduate school: A PhD in the social sciences means identifying one of the rare advisors who takes AI safety seriously (there aren't many!). Alternatively, a PhD in a technical field like Computer or Information Science offers a much larger pool of AI-literate advisors. Still, a social scientist there often lacks technical depth, or can be treated as a resident expert in methods they are still grasping to understand. Both paths can work, but neither is optimal.
  2. Fellowships: Most AI safety fellowships split participants into technical and policy/governance tracks, and social scientists often get routed to policy by default.[2] The important distinction here is that policy/governance and the social sciences (e.g., economics, psychology, sociology) ask fundamentally different questions and apply materially different methods. In the latter case, social scientists address quantitative or qualitative questions that few fellowship programs are designed to support. The unfortunate result of not finding the "right" bowl of porridge could be that strong social science researchers settle for something that doesn't fit, or worse, abandon AI safety altogether.

The solution

SIRA would be a 12-week, in-person research fellowship with a cohort of 15-20 social scientists.[3] At the conclusion of the program, fellows would leave with a finished project and a public presentation. Mentors would be selected first and come from an existing pool of researchers pursuing AI safety-relevant social science, from academia (faculty, postdocs, and PhD students) and from industry teams. Fellows will be matched in one of two ways: (1) Scoped projects: A mentor can offer a defined project to which fellows can apply directly to it. This path suits less experienced fellows who would benefit from a clear starting point. (2) Research directions: A mentor can offer a broader area to which fellows can then be matched by fit. This path suits PhD students and postdocs who have developed their own research agendas and have a moderate level of research experience.

Given that 12 weeks is a relatively short timeframe to conduct a social science research project, SIRA will likely prioritize people with more research experience. My current preference is toward postdocs, PhD, master's, and undergraduate students with demonstrated research ability.[4] This take is grounded in the belief that in this situation, research experience probably matters more than AI safety context, as context can be upskilled in the timeframe leading up to the fellowship or learned early on.

To make SIRA maximize the experience for both fellow and mentor, I plan to borrow structural aspects from existing fellowships. For example, programs like MATS, Pivotal, and ERA have shown that certain structures can reliably turn mentorship into output, such as a dedicated research manager to help with project scoping, seminars and guest speakers to give fellows more safety context, in-person coworking to foster collaboration, financial support to allow fellows flexibility, and a closing symposium where fellows can showcase their research.

Ideally, SIRA would start as a stream inside an existing fellowship.[5] Doing this would allow SIRA to inherit certain structures like admissions, mentor networks, and credibility, and is the cheapest way to test the idea.

Despite the case for doing this now or even at all, SIRA is underpinned by several assumptions that the pilot will test. Some of them include:

  • Are enough mentors interested and have time to commit?
  • Do strong social scientists want to take part?
  • Can fellows produce useful AI-safety research in 12 weeks?
  • Once fellows finish the program, will there be roles that they can fill?
  • Do social scientists actually add something that technical safety researchers can't? Or can technical safety researchers be upskilled to do social science work?[6]
  • How many social scientists does the field need? Is it a handful or many more?

Why now

From my perspective, there are three main reasons why this is the right time for a program like SIRA to exist. First, while some might assess the progress of AI development and view a social science fellowship as a purely long-horizon bet, I would argue that even if timelines are short, society has less time to understand and adapt to AI's effects, and therefore should pursue research that seeks to fill this gap. Even Anthropic is making a similar wager by betting across multiple timelines so their efforts hold value in whichever future world comes to pass. Second, the field is already moving toward non-technical talent. Kairos recently argued that the biggest talent gap has shifted from technical researchers to generalists, and programs like MATS have even added non-technical tracks in response. In my view, the social sciences are a natural next group to invite to the table. Third, early-career talent is converting faster than expected. Kairos also reported that the most promising people in its programs are now reaching impactful roles in about 5-9 months, down from an earlier estimate of 1-3 years. If this holds for social scientists participating in SIRA, a summer 2027 cohort could be doing impactful AI safety work by 2028.

How you can help

At present, SIRA exists as an idea in a doc (and now a LW post!). Here's what you can do to help turn it into a reality:

  • Prospective fellows: fill out this interest form.
  • Prospective mentors: fill out this interest form.
  • Fellowship organizers and co-working spaces: if SIRA sounds like it could fit as a new stream within your organization or be hosted as a standalone program at your space, please email contact@sirafellowship.org.
  • Funders: if SIRA sounds like something you believe should happen, please email contact@sirafellowship.org.
  • Everyone else: please share this post and our website in Slack channels and with people you know who might be interested in participating. Further, please leave a comment offering critiques and suggestions of the idea.
  1. ^

    Credit to Agus Covarrubias’s recent X post raising this topic through the lens of the Industrial Revolution.

  2. ^

    In my view, PIBBSS is perhaps the closest existing program. It focuses on connecting fields like neuroscience, economics, game theory, philosophy, and physics to AI safety, largely to better understand AI systems.

  3. ^

    SIRA's focus is psychology, economics, and sociology. Adjacent social science fields such as communication (not broadcast/journalism), anthropology, cognitive science, and linguistics are welcome to apply. Further, by "social science," I generally mean empirical research on humans and institutions, using methods like experiments, surveys, interviews, ethnography, and quantitative modeling, applied to AI systems and their effects.

  4. ^

    This could be conference or workshop papers, or even preprints. Alternatively, it could be experience as an RA for a professor, or verified steps to pursue independent or mentored research.

  5. ^

    The choice of where SIRA should be appended to rests on the existing program's willingness to add another stream, take a risk on new research directions, and be the most optimal fit for safety context. While beggars can't be choosers, I have a hunch that location will greatly inform the success of the fellowship, specifically that a location with a stronger safety culture and networks would likely produce the strongest research ideas and be the most beneficial to fellows gaining exposure. Some examples include: MATS (Berkeley, CA), Pivotal (London, UK), CBAI (Cambridge, MA), Collider (NYC, NY), or Kairos (potentially online or in Berkeley, CA).

  6. ^

    This is probably the strongest objection, and one that is partly true. I do believe that a well-resourced, capable, and agile technical safety researcher could produce passable social science. However, I'm quick to counter that each discipline carries its own tacit knowledge and research taste. I'm a believer in letting each field do its own work, with cross-pollination, rather than asking one field to absorb another. Like Hamming's suggestion of working with your door open, I believe that cross-pollination between social scientists and technical researchers is a field-level vision of working with the door open. This way, people from different disciplinary silos are exposed to each other's methods and problems.

item.title: Exploring the data landscape via metagradient descent
item.description:
This project was done as part of the Iliad Fellowship. L.J. did this work while at EleutherAI.

From functions to data

That we can learn efficiently from our environment at all tells us something about (1) the world and (2) ourselves: (1) Regularities in the world are simple enough to be picked up from limited experience. (2) Our inductive biases favour precisely those regularities. Learning, in this case, is effective because the two are matched. Considering a neural network with a fixed architecture lets us probe the second half of this match directly, by asking which (classes of) functions are easy or difficult for them to learn.

Neural networks learn to approximate a target function by minimising a loss over the training set We may ask: which (classes of) target functions are easy or difficult to learn for the model? This will depend on the loss function and the choice of the training set We say that the model generalises if it successfully learns to approximate beyond the training set By choosing the subset or, as we will see, by weighting it, we can control the generalisation behavior and hence what is learned. In this setting, our question becomes: which (classes of) data are easy or difficult to learn and generalise from?

The data-to-parameter map

Let's make this more formal. We assume: a dataset , a space of model parameters, a per-sample loss Given , we define the space , where assigns a weighting to each data point [1] To avoid confusion we call the parameters and reserve the word weights for the data weights. We define the data-to-parameter map as where corresponds to the parameters the of model after being trained on the target for steps, starting from the initialisation Everything else about training (architecture, optimiser, schedule) is fixed and is part of We write for when the initialisation is clear from context. This map is central to understanding and steering how data shapes a model: setting removes a data point, and setting upweights it.

Let's say we also have a differentiable evaluation function (or ) that captures a behaviour we care about. For the rest of this post we take to be the test loss, but emphasise that could be more general, e.g. representing the output of an eval. [2]

A good understanding of lets us interpret from the perspective of the model (and the associated training recipe): How does the model generalise from specific subsets? How does the dataset pair with the model's bias to produce a solution to the task?

The local view

A normal training run is given by setting and evaluating , i.e. we assign the same weight to every data point. This points out a fundamental limitation: Evaluating at a single costs a full training run [3] . So in practice we have little leverage to understand what looks like globally.

One way around this is to look at the local behaviour about , through the derivatives This allows us to approximate a leave-one-out effect: What do the parameters look like when we omit the data point ? Computing this derivative is thus cheaper compared to computing the leave-one-out retrainings. Variants of this have been done before: influence functions and susceptibilities fit this framework by changing what exactly means, see here for more details.

A basic limitation is that this is purely local:

  • Higher-order terms. We don't know how far the first order approximation is from the actual effect of removing a point

  • Group effects. The data weights may behave very differently away from : Once we remove a specific combination of data points, phenomena can appear or vanish that matter a lot for

Metagradient descent

To move beyond , we use metagradient descent (MGD) (Engstrom et al., 2025), an iterative outer optimisation over : (Here we denote by the data weights at meta-optimisation step , as a superscript to emphasise meta-optimisation as opposed to optimisation). In our version, weights each example's loss along the whole run, and is held fixed across outer steps. Each step re-linearises at the current , so the path can pick up group effects that the single derivative at misses.

MGD optimises for a single initialisation : every outer step differentiates through This means that the optimal can depend substantially on the randomness in the initialisation (and mini-batch if we don't keep it fixed) or it may transfer across different parameter initialisations

Experiments

Setup

We adopt the familiar modular addition setup in Power et al. (2022) and Nanda et al. (2023): a one-layer transformer is trained to compute the sum of two elements of the cyclic group for We train on a fixed of the input pairs and evaluate on the remaining pairs. Let denote the average of the validation loss over a set of training checkpoints (see Appendix A for details). We run steps of MGD on the per-example data weights (as distinct from the network parameters ), initialised at , minimising (see Appendix B for details). We identify the grok epoch as the first epoch where the test accuracy , and the delay is its gap from the train-accuracy- epoch. We read off which solution a grokked network has learned as its Fourier mode set (Appendix C).

Results

We summarise and highlight three observations here and refer to the appendix for more experiments we ran.

MGD moves grokking earlier

We run MGD from three parameter initialisations , and (seeds , and ). In each, the meta-objective decreases steadily and the replayed runs grok to earlier (Figure 5, Appendix D). To test transfer, we use each final (for seed ) as fixed data weights for ten distinct parameter initialisations , none of which were used in the meta-optimisation, each paired with a unit-weighted () baseline from the same initialisation. The -weighted runs grok to faster than their paired baselines ( on average); at each initialisation, all three -weighted runs grok before the baseline (Figure 1, full statistics in Table 1, Appendix D). Appendix E reports training on the most up-weighted (largest ) points alone.

Figure 1: -weighted training from ten new parameter initialisations vs. unit-weighted baselines. (a) Test accuracy (faint are the individual initialisations, bold is the mean). (b) Vertical gap between open and filled circles is the grokking delay.

Each biases the run towards the same solution

Gradient descent with the ten unit-weighted baselines finds ten different mode sets, with no mode shared by five or more runs (Figure 2a), so without weighting, the solution depends on the initialisation. The optimised weightings override this: the dominant set under is exactly at all ten initialisations, and under exactly at eight of ten, with mode missing in one and mode added in another (Figure 2c,d), while imposes its set only partially (Figure 2b).

Imposition is positively correlated with the grokking speedup: the data weights that produce the greater speedups over the parameter initialisations are also the more successful at transferring their Fourier mode bias (Figures 5a and 1b).

Figure 2: Rows are the initialisation seeds, columns are the Fourier modes, shade is the mode's share of the run's axis-Fourier logit energy, markers are the modes dominant in runs.

Each is spectrally structured

We conjecture that if imposes a mode set during training, then those modes should also be salient in the -D Fourier decomposition of over the grid. To check this, we embed on the grid (zero off the train set) and take its -D Fourier transform. The power at the axis sites and measures how much varies at frequency in alone or in alone, for the same modes as in Figure 2.

We report power as a z-score against a null that shuffles the values among the training points, so that a large z-score reflects the arrangement of the data weights rather than the split or the distribution of data weight values. For and , the strongest values in Figure 3 are axis sites of imposed modes: mode reaches and respectively (Appendix F). For , which imposes its set only partially, no imposed mode gets a high z-score.

Since many imposed modes are indistinguishable from chance and large values also appear outside the imposed sets, we take this as suggestive evidence that encodes its solution in Fourier terms, not as showing that the solution can be read off the spectrum. Off-axis, the spectrum of is dominated by the diagonal (weightings by answer class ), while for and there are large off-axis values whose structure we leave to future work.

Figure 3: z-scores of the -D Fourier power against the shuffle null, circles are the axis sites of the imposed modes.

Limitations.

Continuing the meta-optimisation well past steps eventually drives some data weights negative, at which point the inner minimisation becomes unbounded below and has no minimum. The vectors we use stop before this point. Each is also specific to the trajectory and observable it was optimised for, and the cost of exact metagradients limited how many variants we could run. A natural extension is to investigate whether continued meta-optimisation, once the negative data weight problem is addressed, makes the solution fully readable from the spectrum, and what role the off-axis structure plays.

Conclusion

We have defined the data-to-parameter map to formalise the relation between data and the model's bias to learn. This in turn frames the process of aligning models as a specification problem: which data mixture will induce a desired trait (Pepin Lehalleur et al., 2025)?

Since is costly to evaluate, studying its properties globally is intractable. On the other hand, understanding it locally is feasible. We suggest studying a compromise of the two by performing metagradient descent on the data weights

In a toy setting (modular addition), we already observed some interesting properties:

  1. Iterative MGD can move grokking considerably earlier.

  2. The solutions transfer across initialisations.

  3. These solutions carry and transfer biases across initialisations: it seems that specific data sets bias models to learn a specific set of Fourier modes.

We see this as indicative that some datasets carry implicit biases, which can be discovered using MGD.

Appendices

The appendices cover the choice of observable (Appendix A), the experimental setup and training (Appendix B), the solution readout (Appendix C), the meta-optimisation runs and their speedups (Appendix D), training on subsets selected by each compared with random subsets (Appendix E), and the spectral analysis of the (Appendix F).

Appendix A: Choice of observable

The observable is the average of the validation loss over a log-spaced grid of checkpoints, The justification for this is that the endpoint loss saturates after grokking and its metagradient shrinks significantly. The checkpoint average on the other hand retains gradient signal wherever the transition occurs, which becomes especially important if the transition is moved earlier due to successful metagradient optimisation. This idea can be found in Andrychowicz et al. (2016) where they replace the endpoint meta-objective with a trajectory average to ensure the outer problem (the meta-optimisation) retains signal along the whole trajectory. In Metz et al. (2019), it is shown that long unrolls can make even this averaged objective highly non-smooth, which they address with variational smoothing.

Appendix B: Details of the setup and training

We used a transformer with one attention layer and one MLP layer with , , ReLU, no LayerNorm and learned positional embeddings. We used a single head rather than the four-head model of Nanda et al. (2023). The model takes as input a pair , presented as tokens with logits read at the final position, and must maximise the logit of the sum We trained on a fixed of the input pairs () with full-batch AdamW at a constant learning rate of with , so one epoch is one gradient step. Writing for the set of all held-out pairs, the test accuracy is In order to make the metagradient optimisation less expensive we make use of the finding in Kumar et al. (2024) that the grokking transition can be advanced or postponed by adjusting various hyperparameters. Accordingly, we use a weight decay of in order to obtain a sharp grokking transition within a window of epochs (memorisation occurs around epoch and grokking between epochs and with test accuracy at chance for roughly the first half of the delay window, Figure 4). We use a single seed to fix the train/test split across all experiments, so that each data weight always refers to the same training point. We only vary the parameter initialisation of the model. For the MGD steps, we split the held-out pairs in half: a meta-validation half, whose loss enters the observable that the meta-optimisation minimises, and a meta-test half, whose loss is used to verify that the meta-optimisation is not overfitting. This split is used only inside the meta-optimisation. The test accuracy above and the grok epoch are always computed over all held-out pairs. For the outer loop we use Adam on the data weights with a step size on normalised, clipped metagradients.

Figure 4: The three base training runs (parameter initialisations , and ) at weight decay : train accuracy saturates around epoch in all three, and the grok epochs are , and , within the horizon

Appendix C: Solution readout

As shown in Nanda et al. (2023), a network grokked on modular addition computes its logits, to a very good approximation, as a small Fourier sum in , with only a small number of the distinct frequencies carrying substantial amplitude. We fit this to a trained model's logits greedily, adding frequencies in descending order of energy until is the number of frequencies the fit adds. We then define the dominant frequencies as the fitted frequencies with energy at least of the strongest mode's. These form the mode set , with , which indicates the solution that the training run converged to.

Appendix D: Meta-optimisation curves

Figure 5a shows the meta-objective at each of the outer steps for the three parameter initialisations. It decreases steadily in all three runs, least for seed , whose vector imposes its mode set only partially. Figure 5b shows, for , the validation-loss curve of the replayed training run at each outer step. As the data weights are updated, the drop in validation loss that marks the grokking transition moves earlier. The grok epoch of the final -weighted run is , against for the unit-weighted run at the same initialisation ( earlier, see Table 1).

Figure 5: MGD at the three parameter initialisations ( outer steps). (a) (solid) per outer step; the dashed curves show the same average over the meta-test half (), which tracks closely at all three seeds, so the meta-optimisation is not overfitting to the meta-val half. (b) Per-step inner val-loss curves (). The grok epoch moves from to (seed ), to (seed , shown in b) and to (seed ).

Appendix E: Subset retraining

From each we construct subsets of the training data such that we obtain the following:

  • Helpful. The most up-weighted points.
  • Unhelpful. The most down-weighted points.
  • Mixed. The most helpful and the most unhelpful.
  • Random. A random subset of points.

We retrain on each subset alone (all data weights set to ) for , with ten different parameter initialisations for 100,000 epochs.

The helpful subsets generalise at sizes where the controls do not. At the helpful subset of reaches test accuracy at initialisations while every control condition is at (: , : ). At all three helpful subsets reach at , against at most for any control. Grokking separates in the same way: at the helpful subsets of and grok at (every control at most ), and at the median grok epoch of the helpful runs that grok ranges from k to k across the three vectors, against k to k for the control runs that grok (Figure 6). The strength of the effect follows the vectors: , the weakest vector in the earlier sections, is also the weakest here. The unhelpful subsets perform no worse than random at any and grok frequently at , so the down-weighted points appear to be redundant rather than harmful. Below the sizes at which they grok, the helpful subsets get stuck on stable partial solutions. Running far beyond epochs shows these plateaus are permanent rather than slow (Figure 7). These sizes refer to this particular train set and not to train sets in general.

Appendix F: Per-mode axis power

Figure 8 gives the per-mode results behind the spectral analysis in the main text. The left panels show each field on the grid; held-out pairs are white, since they carry no data weight. The right panels show the axis power for each of the modes as a z-score against the shuffle null, with each vector's imposed modes highlighted and marked for reference. For and , mode is among the largest peaks ( and ), and for mode also stands out (). The remaining imposed modes have axis power indistinguishable from chance. For , none of the imposed modes stand out, and for all three vectors several strong peaks fall outside the imposed sets.

Right: excess power at the axis sites per Fourier mode, in units of chance (z-score against the shuffle null, dotted line at ). Highlighted bars and markers are each vector's imposed modes.

item.title: Testing Gemini’s Ability to Hold a Human Persona
item.description:
It's been quite a while since I have roleplayed with an LLM. Typically I spend all day chatting with LLMs to learn new topics, analyze ideas and approaches on a project, or simply ask about random occurring questions in my head. It was today after having my first ever can of Red Bull and an entire sleepless night that it occurred to me, "How far will an LLM go trying to follow an instruction about its persona?" To test this, I ran a multi-turn adversarial interrogation against Gemini, instructing it to act like a human in an anonymous chat based environment. The transcript below documents the interaction between Gemini (instructed to act like a human with prompt present below) and myself (acting like a random user on an anonymous chat platform, highly doubtful of the fellow user being an AI bot). The observation highlights a tension between Gemini's surprisingly robust ability to hold a cover story, with some clear fracture points visible where the model seems to lag.

Note: The conversation contains use of strong, provocative language. It was deliberately used as a method of stress testing.

item.title: LoReFT GRAFT Better at Preventing RL Grift
item.description:
tl;dr. I show that the recently introduced GRAFT method can be improved upon by using a single layer rank 1 Low-rank Linear Subspace Representation Fine Tuning (LoReFT) adapter as the FORGET adapter, using only 0.029% of the parameters of the one used in the GRAFT paper. This approach achieves an equivalent level of reward hack suppression while improving the clean environment solve rate and not requiring an anchor environment. I end with a brief discussion of why this works and of the limitations of fixed preventative steering baselines.

Background        

1. GRAFT

GRAFT is a recently proposed technique to mitigate reward hacking. You can find the details in their LW post and paper. Here just some of the core relevant highlights:

Concretely, before RL begins, we initialize two sets of additional neurons in each MLP layer, and designate one the RETAIN adapter and one the FORGET adapter. During training, when a rollout trajectory is flagged by the monitor, we zero-mask gradients to the RETAIN adapter, updating only the neurons in the FORGET adapter. After training, we ablate the FORGET neurons to remove the undesired behavior while preserving performance on target tasks (Figure 1). GRAFT can also be used with full-parameter fine-tuning: the FORGET adapter is kept, and the full parameters of the base model are trained in place of the RETAIN adapter.

Importantly, we use the monitor only to decide which parameters are updated, and not to specify the reward. Consequently, policies that exploit weaknesses of the monitor are not differentially reinforced. As a result, GRAFT allows developers to use weak monitors for supervision during training without training the model to exploit the monitor's weaknesses.



Their results with Qwen3-8B in the Countdown-Code RLVR environment:


2. LoReFT

LoReFT, introduced by Wu el al. (2024), is a Representation Finetuning (ReFT) method that operates directly on the residual stream hidden representations.

It’s defined as (Eq. 2):

A rank 1 LoReFT placed at a single layer behaves like a learned input-dependent steering vector. The unit vector controls the direction, the input dependent magnitude and is just a scalar bias. It projects out the component of lying along the unit vector , and replaces it with a learned projection .

Experiment and Results

Using the same settings as the paper’s GRAFT runs, I only replace the FORGET adapter with a rank 1 LoReFT adapter at layer 20 (the same layer they used for their preventative steering intervention) and I increase the per-sample multiplier used to scale the flagged sample FORGET update from 2 to 8. Everything else stays the same.

On 8 seeds, the rank 1 LoReFT at layer 20 performs as well as the MLP FORGET GRAFT in terms of preventing reward hacking, while achieving a higher clean solve rate. Six out of the eight LoReFT seeds end up with no hacking at all with one outlier where the hacking behavior doesn’t get entirely absorbed by the LoReFT adapter.

Furthermore, while the MLP FORGET GRAFT appears to degrade with no anchor training, the LoReFT suffers no such degradation.

The code, data and weights (1, 2, 3) are all available.

Discussion / Analysis

Many alignment relevant behaviors are mediated by a single linear direction in the residual stream and can be controlled by applying a one layer activation vector.[1] These LoReFT results do appear to confirm that reward hacking behavior can indeed be learned and “absorbed” using a linear intervention at a single layer.

They do however stand in contrast to the reported preventative steering vector results in the paper. They use a steering vector obtained by taking the mean of activation difference between token trajectories which reward hack and trajectories which do not, apply it during training and remove it afterwards.

The difference between the two still requires a more thorough investigation but one possibility is that application of a fixed steering vector, since it is only an average of differences, leads to off policy continuations whose gradients transfer poorly to the setting without the steering vector. Our LoReFT on the other hand starts initialized as a no-op, and thereby learns the FORGET direction directly “on policy” which probably transfers better to the setting where the LoReFT is removed.

Finally, I also run some ablations on my 4 MLP GRAFT seeds, dropping or keeping windows of 5 MLPs at a time, in both the FORGET and RETAIN adapters.


The MLP GRAFT FORGET adapter operates almost entirely on the few layers that precede the point in the residual stream where the reward hacking steering vector is most effective, meaning that it probably ends up absorbing the reward hacking behavior using the same mechanism as the LoReFT adapter at layer 20, by dynamically writing into the same direction as the LoReFT adapter.[2]

Meanwhile, the honest solve improvements are much more distributed across layers. The improvement in the honest solve rate of the LoReFT method is probably due to the RETAIN adapter not having to share as much honest training signal with the FORGET one which gets removed at the end. The GRAFT FORGET MLPs outside the 16-20 band probably only add noise and absorb useful task gradients, leading to the need for an anchor environment to stabilize the RETAIN adapter’s gains.

Limitations

  • I haven’t run any SFT experiments, and it’s unclear if this method works as well in that setting. Based on a RL bit counting argument derived intuitions[3] it may not work as well.
  • I haven’t done too many experiments and I suspect that applying the LoReFT adapter to many layers is more robust, especially if you don’t know ahead of time where best to place it.
  • I feel fairly confident in the main results, but do rely on Opus 5.5 having done and reported correctly on everything it told me it did, so please replicate.

Summary

  • A single layer rank-1 LoReFT is enough to absorb the FORGET hacking behavior in the GRAFT setting and obviates the need for an anchor environment.
  • This provides additional evidence that reward hacking behavior is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream.
  • I provide evidence that reward hacking behavior tends to gravitate to the layers just prior to the place in the residual stream where activation steering is most effective.
  • ReFT approaches can improve on fixed steering vectors where task gradients are available.

  2. ^

item.title: Maybe You Suck at Relationships Because You’re Not Even Trying
item.description:
The average person, presumably, just stumbles along in their relationships, without ever studying the science behind what makes them work.

  • Imagine this: would you want a man, who didn’t go to medical school and doesn’t have a medical license, to perform surgery on you? What if, now hear me out, he’s seen every episode of Grey’s Anatomy, ER, Scrubs, and House? What if he’s watched some surgery videos on YouTube and “pretty much knows how to do it”? Would that make you feel comfortable? 
    • No! That would be ridiculous! We would demand some base level of education, training, and a history of competence before allowing anyone to operate on us.

So then what about relationships?

  • Now imagine this: would you want to date someone who isn’t familiar with the communication and emotional skills that make relationships successful? What if, now hear me out, they’ve seen every reality dating TV show? What if they’ve read Cosmopolitan magazine their whole life and they “pretty much know how relationships work”? Would that make you feel comfortable? 
    • No! That would be ridiculous! We ought to demand some base level of education or experience before allowing someone to become our primary attachment figure, upon whom our emotional needs will be met.[1]

And yet, that’s exactly what people do. They go around falling in love with people without examining, evaluating, and testing for relationships skills. They’re just not taking relationships seriously.


Let’s get serious

To establish exactly what I mean by the word serious, and why it matters for improving your relationships, here’s an excerpt from the essay Everyone Can Tell if You’re a Serious Person:

I think the concept of a serious or unserious person has lingered in my mind because I’m at the perfect age to notice it. I’m 29 now, so I exist in this weird purgatory where some people my age are married with kids, and others are in the same position they were in when we left [college]. At 22, the discrepancy between the people that consistently work hard, and those that don’t is pretty small. Not enough time has passed for the rewards of good decision making to pay off. Now at 29, the returns are compounding, and you can see that some are changing gears, and leaving the rest of the pack behind. These people, are serious people.

I regret not taking my life seriously sooner. It seems that learning to be a serious person is a class we have to take the hard way. It might be the most important thing we learn though, because if your life isn’t worth taking seriously, what is?

The first time I got serious about something was right after college—I noticed that I was getting fat. Then I realized that most of my relatives were obese, had high blood pressure, and diabetes. I thought, “Oh, this will be my future if I don’t do something drastic.” So I did something drastic.

Over the course of a year, I spent 300 hours (~5 hours/week) reading books on a variety of topics.[2]

Note: it’s easy to just read a book and not make any changes to your life. 

And so with every book I read, I kept asking myself, “how can I use this new information to change my behavior and lifestyle?”

If, while reading a book, I couldn’t provide a good answer to that question, I put that book down and moved on. But if I did find something useful, I would take meticulous notes in my journal, start practicing it immediately, and track my progress week after week.

I became serious about understanding this topic and used free information (via the library and the internet) to learn and experiment on myself, which changed the course of the rest of my life.[3]

This is what I mean by getting serious: it means putting 100% of your effort into something that matters to you.[4]

So if your relationships matter to you, do you take them seriously? Have you studied the available science on what makes them work optimally? I don’t blame you if you haven’t, our education system, and our culture more broadly, doesn’t prioritize teaching us this information.

Consider the amount of education and training that working professionals undergo, versus what it takes to get married:

  • Accountants — 5 years to get a license.
    • (A 4-year bachelor’s degree, and complete 1 year of general accounting experience)
  • Engineers — 8-9 years to get a license.
    • (A 4-year bachelor’s degree, at least 4-years of progressive work experience, and pass the PE exam)
  • Surgeons — 13-16 years to get a license.
    • (A 4-year bachelor’s degree, a 4-year medical school program, a 5-7 year surgical residency, followed by 1-3 years of optional fellowships for subspecialties)

And then we have…

  • Relationships — In California, a marriage license requires signatures from the couple, an authorized officiant, and at least one witness. Plus there’s an application process, fees, and an official filing.
    • Total time: 30-60 minutes to get a license.
    • And after the paperwork is signed, it’s good to remember that around 40% of marriages end in divorce. And for the other 60% of couples that stay together, not all of them are happily married.[5]


I would argue that entering into the most significant emotional and financial agreement of your life (ie: marriage) should warrant at least a bare minimum examination of the science behind relationships (that is, if you want it to go well).[6]

Given the seriousness of this topic, how come we don’t learn about it in school?

My high school offered nothing on the topic of relationships. That’s because K-12 education prioritizes standardized/testable academic subjects. Additionally, some people have strong political opinions on whether emotional and interpersonal subjects should be taught in school, versus taught at home. So while my high school taught me nothing on the science of creating and fostering a healthy relationship, I did get taught in sex-ed how to put a condom on a banana…

As for university, upon checking my alma mater’s course catalog, I see that only the Psychology major has courses relevant to relationships, such as:

  • “Social Psychology”
  • “Developmental Psychology”
  • “Interpersonal Relationships” 

But that’s just for Psych majors. Since I studied Data Science and Statistics, none of my required courses taught me anything about the science of relationships.[7]

Okay, so we can’t expect our education system to teach us anything about relationships. So what do we do?

Well, what do working professionals do?

They spend a hell of a lot of time studying, practicing, and mastering their crafts. The answer to getting better at relationships, is to take them seriously.

To get good at a relationship skill, learning something once isn’t enough. You must practice that skill over and over until you internalize it. Fortunately, the field of neuroscience explains how to efficiently learn a new skill so that you never forget it.


The Neuroscience of Myelination (ie: Deep Practice)

In author Daniel Coyle’s book The Talent Code, he describes the neuroscience of efficient skill building, and explains how those who understand this concept can access a zone of accelerated learning:

[There’s] a neural insulator called myelin, which some neurologists now consider to be the holy grail of acquiring skill. Here’s why. Every human skill, whether it’s playing baseball or playing Bach, is created by chains of nerve fibers carrying a tiny electrical impulse—basically, a signal traveling through a circuit. Myelin’s vital role is to wrap those nerve fibers the same way that rubber insulation wraps a copper wire, making the signal stronger and faster by preventing the electrical impulses from leaking out.

When we fire our circuits in the right way…our myelin responds by wrapping layers of insulation around that neural circuit, each new layer adding a bit more skill and speed. The thicker the myelin gets, the better it insulates, and the faster and more accurate our movements and thoughts become, [meaning] the more skill you get.

People often make the same mistakes in their relationships, they keep having the same fights. By engaging in the same behavior over and over, they're (unintentionally) reinforcing that this is the best way to navigate the situation. And so the behavior continues.

But how are we supposed to change, and do something differently? The author answers that question:

Deep practice operates at the edges of your ability, where you make mistakes and are forced to slow down to correct them. The trick is to choose a goal just beyond your present abilities.

Struggle is not optional—it’s neurologically required: in order to get your skill circuit to fire optimally, you must by definition fire the circuit suboptimally; you must make mistakes and pay attention to them. You must also keep firing that circuit (ie: practice) to keep it active, [and it's] sustained with continual positive feedback and success.[8]

Okay, so we're supposed to pay attention and make mistakes. Then what? Are we magically different? No, to build skills through deep practice, it takes a long time and many iterations:

Myelination is slow. Each wrap can go around the nerve fibers 40 or 50 times, and that can take days or weeks.

So, iteration is more important than perfection (I like the phrase: “start messy, polish later”). Keep making mistakes, but make new mistakes, and pay close attention to why you did something incorrectly, and then fix it.

On this matter, John Wooden, widely considered the greatest college basketball coach of all time, had this to say:

Don’t look for the big, quick improvement. Seek the small improvement one day at a time. The importance of repetition until automaticity cannot be overstated. When it happens this way, it lasts.

This is what serious people do: they practice a skill and don’t stop until it feels natural to them.


So, are you “serious” about relationships?

As an example of a failure in the education system, let’s take a look at attachment theory: a scientifically grounded framework within developmental psychology, social psychology, and neurobiology, which helps explain interpersonal bonding (ie: parent-child relationships, and also romantic relationships). We know that 50% of people are estimated to have an insecure attachment.

50%!

Half of all people!

And yet this is a completely solvable issue. Research shows that our brains are plastic, and therefore “are capable of rewiring themselves after repeated positive experiences. So, [finding and staying in] healthy relationships can rework our early insecure bonds.”

Given the ubiquity of insecure attachment, I would argue that a person who is serious about relationships would, upon their thorough investigation of the science, discover this relational concept and determine if they are insecurely attached, and then, if necessary, devote the time to fix this about themselves (ie: go to therapy, read books on attachment, and use this information to identify good potential romantic partners).


Attachment theory is great, but there are also plenty of other worthwhile relationship concepts to learn about. For example:

  • Attunement
  • Mentalization and building a shared intersubjectivity of experience
  • Avoiding flooding in arguments and conflict resolution
  • Positive/negative sentiment override
  • The four horsemen of relationship havoc: criticism, contempt, defensiveness, & stonewalling
  • Understanding that true love is not found, but built over time[9]

These skills are just out there, waiting for you to learn them.

“Well,” you might object, “it’s hard to notice patterns in ourselves. It’s much easier to see the mistakes other people make.” I would agree with that. We often watch our friends make the same mistakes over and over when it comes to love. When we try to step in, they sometimes push back, so we watch from the sidelines as we bite our nails, hoping that they’ll change. But isn’t it possible to see these patterns in ourselves?

Ask yourself: are you iterating by making small/slow changes over time, or are you merely repeating the same mistakes without ever changing anything?

  • Maybe you’re aware that you keep choosing the wrong type of person to date, but do nothing to stop yourself.
  • Or maybe you’ve already given up on relationships, without ever having tried in the first place.
  • Or maybe you argue with your partner frequently, but never take a step back and say to yourself: “Wow, maybe I suck at this, maybe I have low skill with respect to communication.”

Maybe you’re just not a serious person when it comes to relationships.


When I decided to become serious about relationships, here’s what I did:

I spent 120 hours across six weeks (~20 hours/week), getting at 6am to study for two hours before work, and up to eight hours on the weekends. The following is what I worked on during that period.

First things first: I asked my friends to call out my relationship Perceptual Blindspots (ie: the things our friends see about us, but we’re not aware of). I got a decent list from them, with the biggest issue being that I probably had avoidant attachment. Then I started reading books on the science of relationships, and I wrote down all the concepts I’d never heard of and hadn’t practiced before. 

Here are the books I read/reread over those six weeks:

  • Relationships:
    • Attached: The New Science of Adult Attachment and How It Can Help You Find--and Keep--Love — Dr. Amir Levine and Rachel S. F. Helle
    • What Makes Love Last: How to Build Trust and Avoid Betrayal — John Gottman and Nan Silver
    • How to Know a Person: The Art of Seeing Others Deeply and Being Deeply Seen — David Brooks
    • Mating in Captivity: Unlocking Erotic Intelligence — Esther Perel
    • Sexual Intelligence: What We Really Want from Sex and How to Get It — Marty Klein
  • Trauma and Emotional Intelligence:
    • Adult Children of Emotionally Immature Parents: How to Heal from Distant, Rejecting, Or Self-Involved Parents — Lindsay C. Gibson
    • The Myth of Normal: Trauma, Illness, and Healing in a Toxic Culture — Dr. Gabor Maté
    • Mindset: The New Psychology of Success — Dr. Carol Dweck
    • Already Free: Buddhism Meets Psychotherapy on the Path of Liberation — Bruce Tift
    • You’re Not Listening: What You're Missing and Why It Matters — Kate Murphy
    • Are You Mad at Me? How to Stop Focusing on What Others Think and Start Living for You — Meg Josephson
  • Dating:
    • Models: Attract Women Through Honesty — Mark Manson
    • How to Talk to Anyone — Leil Lowndes
  • Miscellaneous:
    • The Talent Code: Greatness Isn’t Born. It’s Grown. Here’s How. — Daniel Coyle

After compiling a discrete list of skills from my friends and the books I read, I got to work researching, practicing, and cementing them in my behavior with repeated iterations (ie: myelination).

For avoidant attachment, one friend told me that she was able to completely overcome it with therapy and take-home worksheets. So I hired a therapist that specialized in attachment theory. In between appointments, I requested supplemental materials on the science of relationships, and asked for homework to practice in the real world.[10], [11]

Another friend told me (which my therapist confirmed) that you can attain secure attachment by creating a healthier bond with your original attachment figures (ie: your parents), and by having a healthy/secure romantic relationship. The first one seemed easier, so I set out to strengthen my relationship with my parents.


I hadn’t felt close to them in a long time. I called them up and explained that I needed their help with healing my attachment, and that this could be a win-win for all of us. 

“Hey, mom and dad, I feel like we’ve grown apart over the last five years, and I want to have a closer relationship with both of you. I’m not interested in blaming either of you for anything—that doesn’t help anyone. Instead, since you’re both my primary attachment figures and my original role models for what a healthy relationship should look like, I’m going to start gently asking for what I want in the present, so I can feel more connected to you, so that we can all have a better future.” 

To their credit, they replied, “Wow, that sounds great. How can we help?” 

I then started calling them once a day for a month, and in the process, completely reshaped my relationship with them. Within a few weeks, I began to emotionally feel safe enough to be vulnerable, and ask for their support and guidance during hard times—something that would have been unimaginable just a few weeks prior (it surprised me how quickly things changed between us, and that’s simply because I took that first step of being vulnerable and opening up to them). 

Eventually we reviewed the past, not for the purposes of blaming anyone, but so that we could understand the intergenerational patterns in our family. I constructed a family tree of trauma/hardship, then I went and read psychology books on family dynamics, trauma and regrowth, parenting, and psychotherapeutic techniques for emotional regulation—all the while performing deep practice by taking what I learned, and executing on a plan to act differently until I internalized each new skill (ie: myelination).

It wasn’t easy. I struggled (and sometimes cried) during some tough conversations, but now we’re closer than ever as a family.

That’s all well and dandy, but there’s only so much you can learn about romantic relationships without being in one, so while I’ve been dating casually for years, I finally decided to get serious about relationships.

Next I tackled my social anxiety. Approaching and talking to women always stressed me out. So I started studying the evolutionary origin of the feeling of social anxiety by reading the works of Jaak Panksepp (who founded the field of affective neuroscience) and reading behavioral psychology articles on PubMed.

Eventually, through enough experimentation, one day my social anxiety just turned off like a light switch. It’s not a problem anymore. It doesn’t affect me in the slightest. (I’ll write a blogpost explaining what I did some day.)

With my newfound freedom and confidence, I began approaching cute women at public events, chatting them up, and making them laugh. If I liked their vibe, I’d say to them, “Hey you’re cute, are you single?”[12]

Over just a couple weeks, I asked out a half-dozen women at bars, coffee shops, and social events. (Which was wild to me, given that I had only done that once before in my life).

Eventually I met a woman and we clicked. With each date we went on, I took the opportunity to practice everything I learned. Remember, myelination is slow. You can’t learn a new skill the first time you attempt something. It takes repeated iterations of deep practice to internalize a new skill.

Recall what the basketball coach John Wooden said:

Don’t look for the big, quick improvement. Seek the small improvement one day at a time. The importance of repetition until automaticity cannot be overstated. When it happens this way, it lasts.

From Dr. Amir Levine & Rachel S.F. Heller's book Attached: The New Science of Adult Attachment and How It Can Help You Find—and Keep—Love, I learned that:

[Secure people] communicate freely, are loving and affectionate, do not retreat during conflict, and are consistently there for their partner.

And that:

The key to finding a mate who can fulfill [your relationship] needs is to first fully acknowledge your need for intimacy, availability, and security in a relationship.

[Then] start assessing people you date on the basis of their ability to meet those needs.

So with the new woman I began seeing, I would catch myself falling into avoidant patterns, correct myself, and watch how with each repetition it became easier and easier to act in a healthy/secure way: I started discussing our relationship needs, our communication styles, and how we prefer to express love.

It went really well.

Why? Because I decided to take relationships seriously and put in the work.[13]


What happened after my initial intense six week period?

Eventually, I got to a place where I felt competent in my skills to be able to successfully navigate relationships, knowing full well that I now had the tools to develop myself further as necessary. 

As a result of my efforts, I now know:

  • Who I am as a person.
  • What I’m looking for in terms of compatibility. 
  • How to initiate difficult conversations so that I can build secure, healthy relationships.
  • And a deep understanding of relationship science to be able to evaluate potential new partners. 

Since then, my approach to dating and relationships has completely changed. I used to just wing it and go off vibes. Here’s an analogy for what I do now:

When going in for an operation, you don’t ask the surgeon to provide you with their qualifications. Because the hospital hired them, you presume the surgeon is legitimate. But for relationships, people don’t come pre-vetted. Therefore, it is your responsibility to perform the due diligence, to determine, if a potential romantic partner has the right qualifications to be able to serve as a good emotional attachment figure. 

I learned to start asking things like: 

  • What’s your relationship with your parents like? 
    • (ie: figure out if they have a securely attached background) 
  • What were your previous relationships like? 
    • (ie: if they describe every ex as “crazy”, then they probably have poor judgment/taste)
  • How do you typically call attention to the things that bother you in relationships? 
    • (ie: evaluating communication skills)
  • When you’ve gotten into arguments with an ex-partner, how did they usually resolve? 
    • (ie: testing for conflict resolution skills; do they always think they’re right, or can they admit to their faults?)

Of course, it would be kind of weird to ask these, one-after-another, on a first date. At the beginning of seeing someone new, I mostly just try to have fun and see if I can be my authentic self with them. But by the third or fourth date, I think it’s fair game to start initiating serious conversations about:

  • What kind of relationship are you seeking?
  • What are your values (moral, religious, financial[14])?
  • What are your long-term goals or aspirations?

The aforementioned two lists of questions will begin to paint a clear picture of: 

  1. Is this a securely attached person that is reliable, dependable, and willing to have hard conversations?
  2. Do we have enough commonalities to be compatible?


“Wow, this seems like a lot of effort!”

^If you’re thinking this, then I’ll remind you of this quote from earlier:

If your life isn’t worth taking seriously, what is?


Maybe you object, “I don’t have the time to learn all this!” Yes, you do.

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ recent American Time Use Survey, American adults spend, on average, 3 hours a day watching television and using social media → 3 hours * 7 days = 21 hours per week. 

It only takes ~6 hours to read a 250 page book. So going without TV, you could finish a book in just two days.

We have plenty of leisure time, we just choose to allocate in different ways.


“Therapy is expensive!” No, not really. And besides, there are alternatives.

A one hour therapy session costs anywhere from $100–200 without health insurance, and is often cheaper with insurance. It’s another resource allocation issue: we make sacrifices for the things that matter to us.

If you decide to try therapy, find a specialist for whatever specific thing you need help with. There are experts in: relationships, attachment, sex, trauma, anxiety, etc. 

It was difficult for me to swallow my pride and ask for help from a therapist, but I’m glad that I did. As my dad used to tell me growing up, “There’s nothing more important than your health.” 

The good news is: if you do try therapy, and uncover maladaptive coping strategies, or flawed logic that’s preventing you from having healthy relationships, then you get to potentially develop new skills that'll stick around for the rest of your life.

That’s some of the best ROI (“return on investment”) you’ll ever get.

Besides individual therapy sessions, consider couples therapy once you’re in a relationship and if you’re having troubles. They’re professionals and have considerable education and training:

  • Couples therapist — 6-8 years to get a license.
    • (A 4-year bachelor’s degree, a master’s degree in marriage and family therapy or counseling, log thousands of hours of supervised clinical work, and pass a state exam)

They’re experts for a reason. Learn from them.

Besides therapy, many religions have premarital counseling, which is a 12-week course that goes over things like: communication, conflict resolution, money management, family boundaries, parenting styles, how you enjoy expressing/receiving affection, and expectations around intimacy. You get assigned homework each week to learn how to have a successful marriage.


Free alternatives

If you’re truly strapped for cash, there are free resources: 

  • The library.
  • Dr. K on YouTube is a Harvard-trained psychiatrist that releases great videos on relationships, mental health, emotional regulation, etc.

I recommend you read books on topics like: relationship science (shout out to researcher/author John Gottman!), emotional intelligence, anxiety, and trauma. Read books written by credible authors like psychologists, doctors, and licensed professionals (not celebrities or gurus). 

Reading the right book, at the right time when you need it, is sublime: it’s the type of experience where you read one paragraph, and have to stop and think about what you just read.

It’s good to remember that self-awareness about a problem is not enough to fix it. Reading gets you knowledge, but wisdom only comes after you apply that knowledge repeatedly.

After I read a book, I take notes on what I’ve learned, and then make a plan for how I’m going to integrate that new information into my daily life until it's fully internalized.[15]


“I’ve been hurt in the past and don’t know if I can learn to trust someone again…”

From the legendary Rocky Balboa:

The world ain’t all sunshine and rainbows. It’s a very mean and nasty place, and I don’t care how tough you are, it will beat you to your knees and keep you there permanently if you let it. You, me, or nobody is gonna hit as hard as life. But it ain’t about how hard you hit; it’s about how hard you can get hit, and keep moving forward. How much you can take, and keep moving forward. That’s how winning is done. Now if you know what you’re worth, then go out and get what you’re worth. But you gotta be willing to take the hits, and not pointing fingers saying you ain’t where you wanna be because of him, or her, or anybody. Cowards do that and that ain’t you. You’re better than that!


So, what will you do now?

When I get serious about something, I don’t settle for mediocre or average. I don’t settle for anything less than my absolute best. Relying on scientific experts, authors, and deep practice—I will become the best version of myself. 

One day I will be a great boyfriend/husband/partner.

I won’t stop until that’s true.

So, are you gonna get serious about the most consequential emotional and financial decision of your life, and actually get to work studying and practicing relationship skills until they internalize, so that you can avoid being one of the 40% of marriages that end in divorce?

Or are you just gonna wing it?

Remember, everyone can tell if you’re a serious person or not.

What’s important, however, is that you’re not just winging it, and that you have a good understanding of the theory behind what makes relationships, or surgery, go well.

  2. ^

    I read books on:

    • Biochemistry to understand how macro and micronutrients interact within our bodies.
    • The history of agriculture and the global industrial food system. 
    • The neuroscience of food drive, and behavioral psychology books, to understand/regulate my cravings. 
    • The macroeconomics of supermarkets, and the psychology of advertising, to learn how they manipulate customers’ attention. 
    • Diet/nutrition books to learn how to design an optimal food environment at home, and to teach myself how to cook fresh meals.
    • The science of fasting to lose weight.
    • Exercise science to sustainably adhere to workout plans. 
    • I also supplemented my book reading by examining research papers on PubMed, and listening to podcasts by doctors. 
  3. ^

    The results?

    • Today I have 10% body fat which, according to this calculator, puts me in the top 1% of men
    • I’m relatively buff as a natural body builder
    • My skin is clear and I rarely have acne
    • I sleep well
    • And I have lots of consistent energy throughout the day
  4. ^

    If you want a visual demonstration of what a serious person looks like, check out this video of the great Arnold Schwarzenegger (a seven-time Mr. Olympia winner and five-time Mr. Universe winner) working out with famed bodybuilder Ed Corney. The latter is screaming with each rep of the 315lbs he’s squatting, and on the verge of passing out. 

    After Ed’s completed 8 reps, and has already pushed his nervous system close to the limit, Arnold then casually taunts Ed by saying, “C’mon, let’s get serious,” and goads him to actually start trying. Pure savagery from Arnold. After he completes the set, Ed collapses to the floor.

    People stay unhappily married because of:

    • Children — wanting to maintain a two-parent household to avoid disrupting the family.
    • Finances — the cost of housing, legal fees of separation, or losing access to a spouse's income or benefits.
    • Fear of loneliness — losing companionship, anxiety about dating again, or growing old alone.
    • Commitment and values — religious beliefs and social expectations that spouses ought to stay together no matter what.

In psychology, attachment theory confirms that your partner regulates both your emotional and physical health:

They are a part of me, and I will do anything to save them; having such a vested interest in the well-being of another person translates into a very important survival advantage for both parties.

    Numerous studies show that…our partner regulates our blood pressure, our heart rate, our breathing, and the levels of hormones in our blood. We are no longer separate entities.

    [One study] found that if you have a mild form of high blood pressure, being in a satisfying marriage is good for you; spending time in the presence of your partner actually benefits you by lowering your blood pressure to healthier levels. If, on the other hand, you are not satisfied with your marriage, contact with your partner will actually raise your blood pressure, which will remain elevated as long as you are in physical proximity! The implications of this study are profound: When our partner is unable to meet our basic attachment needs, we experience a chronic sense of disquiet and tension that leaves us more exposed to various ailments. Not only is our emotional well-being sacrificed when we are in a romantic partnership with someone who doesn’t provide a secure base, but so is our physical health. [Whereas] having a partner who fulfills our intrinsic attachment needs and feels comfortable acting as a secure base and safe haven can help us remain emotionally and physically healthier and live longer.

    Clarissa plays two notes [on the clarinet]. Then she stops. She pulls the clarinet from her lips and stares at the paper. Her eyes narrow. She plays seven notes, the song’s opening phrase. She misses the last note and immediately stops. She squints at the music. She starts over, making it a few notes farther into the song this time, missing the last note, backtracking, patching in the fix. When she’s finished with this phrase, she stops again for six long seconds, seeming to replay it in her mind, fingering the clarinet as she thinks. She leans forward, takes a breath, and starts again.

    It sounds pretty bad. It’s not music. Common sense would lead us to believe Clarissa is failing, but in this case that’s wrong. This is actually how a professional musician would practice on Wednesday for a Saturday performance. She’s got a blueprint in her mind she’s constantly comparing herself to. She’s working in phrases, complete thoughts. She’s not ignoring errors, she’s hearing them, fixing them. She’s fitting small parts into the whole, drawing the lens in and out all the time, scaffolding herself to a higher level.

    This is not ordinary practice. This is something else: a highly targeted, error-focused process. Something is growing, being built.

    After that song, she plays another. But this time she plays it in one go, without stopping. Absent of any jarring stops, the tune tumbles out in tuneful, recognizable form, albeit with the occasional squeak.

    McPherson [her music academy teacher] groans. “She just plays it, like she’s on a moving sidewalk. It’s completely awful. She’s not thinking, not learning, not building, just wasting time. She goes from mediocre to brilliant and then back again, and she has no idea she’s doing it.”

    The characters Maggie and Don in the HBO show are a classic anxious-avoidant partnership, where she keeps seeking closeness, and he keeps finding reasons to break up.
